To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
factorization algorithms can be used to identify muscle synergies, and that the performance of different algorithms varies depending on the type of noise in the data set.

(1) the algorithms used for the identification of synergies are not interchangeable; (2) the performance of these algorithms varies across data sets; (3) the performance of the algorithms can be improved by using an ad hoc procedure to determine the number of synergic components; (4) the performance of factorization algorithms can be improved if the data set is preprocessed by principal component analysis; (5) the performance of ICA can be improved by constraining it to be probabilistic,
the algorithms ICA, FA, NMF, pICA, and ICAPCA perform well on data sets with nonnegative values, and are robust against signal-dependent noise and correlated synergy activation coefficients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of muscle synergy patterns from electromyographic (EMG) signals.
the identification of a set of muscle synergies underlying a behavior.
the identification of muscle synergy patterns in human motor behavior.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ICA is a good method for identifying synergies, but that it should be used with caution in the presence of signal-dependent noise.
the algorithms are able to extract the synergies from the data, but the synergies themselves are not a function of the algorithm used to extract them, but rather a function of the data itself.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the muscle synergistic organization of muscle activation pattern is robust to different factorization algorithms and noise conditions.
factorization algorithms are a powerful tool to study muscle synergy organization, but the results obtained from them should be interpreted in light of the specific properties of the algorithms used.
ICA is a powerful tool to analyze muscle activation data, especially when combined with PCA to define the subspace of interest.
